personas.summary: Not-go as it stands, but the gap to publishable is small and surgical. This is the most chemically careful carbohydrate chapter I have reviewed here: I parsed all 30 molecule SMILES in assets[] plus all 34 distinct SMILES in question student_config with RDKit, assigned CIP labels, and additionally hydrolysed all four disaccharides in silico against verified monosaccharide references - maltose, cellobiose, lactose and sucrose are all correct in sugar identity, linkage carbon AND anomeric configuration, which is where chapters of this kind normally fail. Every numeric claim I could check is right, and the authoring even gets the hard details right - ribitol is correctly named without a D- prefix while D-arabinitol is correctly chiral, and the chapter's own 'beta = same face as the reference arm' rule survives the furanose test I ran on beta-D-fructofuranose in 3D. Three things block assignment. (1) mol-beta-d-xylopyranose is drawn as alpha-D-xylopyranose, so the one figure the chapter uses to make its all-equatorial point shows an axial anomeric hydroxyl and contradicts its own caption, the prose, and a question key. (2) The comparison_matrix answer key asserts that free beta-D-glucopyranose survives prolonged 1 M NaOH, flatly contradicting the Lobry de Bruyn-van Ekenstein passage the same chapter teaches two sections later. (3) The chapter's closing claim that humans secrete no beta-glucosidase at all is an exceptionless rule the chapter itself breaks by naming lactase. Separately, the question bank is positionally guessable: every single_select keys to option 'a', every matching_pairs is perfectly diagonal, every rank_order ships pre-sorted, and every structured_reasoning claim is both first-listed and longer than its distractors - and I found no shuffling in any renderer.

location.anchor_text: A pentose whose pyranose ring, like that of beta-D-glucopyranose, places every substituent equatorial.

findings.observation: The SMILES on mol-beta-d-xylopyranose is alpha-D-xylopyranose, not beta. Its anomeric configuration is inverted relative to the named compound. Two independent checks agree: its RDKit canonical form matches an alpha reference built by inverting only the anomeric tag of a beta-D-xylopyranose derived from the verified beta-D-glucopyranose asset by deleting C6; and an embedded MMFF-minimised conformer puts the anomeric C-O bond at a ring-normal projection of +1.41 (axial) while true beta-D-xylopyranose gives all four hydroxyls equatorial.
findings.learner_impact: This figure exists solely to make the chapter's headline structural argument - that a ring can put every substituent equatorial. The drawing a student sees shows the anomeric hydroxyl axial, so the figure disproves the caption printed beneath it, the asset long_description, the nugget prose, and the answer key of ch25-beta-glucose-chair-v2, which keys 'equatorial'. A student who trusts the figure over the text learns the wrong anomer.
findings.evidence: assets[].id = mol-beta-d-xylopyranose, smiles 'O[C@@H]1[C@@H](O)[C@@H](O)OC[C@H]1O'; correct beta-D-xylopyranose canonicalises to 'O[C@@H]1[C@@H](O)[C@H](O)OC[C@H]1O'. The compiled reader carries the same string. Question ch25-beta-glucose-chair-v2 answer_key [redacted].
findings.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs the figure that its all-equatorial-pentose argument depends on to actually be the beta anomer, so that the drawing, the caption, the accessible description, the prose claim and the chair question key all describe the same molecule.

location.anchor_text: Survives prolonged treatment with 1 M aqueous NaOH at room temperature

findings.observation: The answer key marks feature f_base as 'yes' for case_sugar (free beta-D-glucopyranose): the free sugar is asserted to survive prolonged 1 M aqueous NaOH at room temperature. It does not. A free reducing sugar in 1 M hydroxide opens to the aldehyde, is deprotonated alpha to the carbonyl, and equilibrates through the 1,2-enediol - the Lobry de Bruyn-van Ekenstein rearrangement - giving a mixture of D-glucose, D-mannose and D-fructose, with further base-mediated degradation on standing. The chapter teaches exactly this two sections later and draws exactly the opposite conclusion from it.
findings.learner_impact: A student who has read nugget-sugar-oxidation-and-reduction and correctly answers 'does not apply' is graded wrong, and the feedback then reinforces the error: the level-3 hint states 'Neither compound has an acidic proton or a leaving group that hydroxide can act on', which is false for the free sugar whose open-chain form has an acidic C2-H. The item destroys the chapter's own best argument for why glycosides are used as anomeric protecting groups.
findings.evidence: ch25-anomer-comparison-v2 answer_key [redacted]. Contradicted by nugget-sugar-oxidation-and-reduction expanded text and by nugget-glycoside-formation.
findings.recommended_outcome: The base-stability row needs to discriminate the two compounds the way the chapter's chemistry actually does - the glycoside survives, the free hemiacetal does not - and the accompanying feedback needs to stop asserting that the free sugar has no base-accessible proton.

location.anchor_text: Humans secrete alpha-glucosidases - salivary and pancreatic amylase, maltase, and the rest - and secrete no beta-glucosidase at all.

findings.observation: This exceptionless claim is stated three times (standard tier, expanded tier, and the nugget practice_check answer) and it is not exceptionless. Humans express lactase-phlorizin hydrolase at the brush border, whose phlorizin-hydrolase domain is a beta-glucosidase and which slowly hydrolyses cellobiose; humans also express cytosolic beta-glucosidase and glucosylceramidase. The chapter contradicts itself two paragraphs earlier by naming lactase as the enzyme that hydrolyses lactose's beta-1,4 linkage. The defensible statement is that humans secrete no cellulase - no endo-beta-1,4-glucanase capable of depolymerising cellulose.
findings.learner_impact: This is the chapter's closing argument and the payoff of its whole stereochemistry-matters thesis, so it is the sentence students will retain. As written it teaches a false absolute that a biochemistry course will have to un-teach, and it is internally inconsistent in a way an attentive student will spot immediately.
findings.evidence: nugget-di-and-polysaccharides standard and expanded tiers plus practice_check answer; same nugget four paragraphs earlier: 'hydrolysing it requires the specific enzyme lactase.'
findings.recommended_outcome: The digestibility contrast needs to be stated as a claim that survives the chapter's own lactase example - humans lack the enzyme that cleaves beta-1,4 glucan chains, not the entire class of beta-glycosidases.

location.observation: The correct answer is encoded in position across essentially the whole bank. All 12 single_select items key to option 'a' (first-listed). Both 5-option multi_selects other than ch25-fischer-legal-manipulations key to the first three options contiguously. All 4 matching_pairs items are perfectly diagonal. Both rank_order items ship their cards already in the correct order, so the answer is the untouched default state. No shuffle, randomise, or Math.random call exists under frontend/src/components/activity-renderers or frontend/src/features/lessonPanel/questions.
location.learner_impact: A student can score well above chance on this bank without doing any chemistry: pick 'a', drag nothing on the ranking items, match straight across, and choose the longest claim. That makes the bank useless as an assessment of the concepts, and rewards test-wiseness over the structural reasoning the chapter is built to teach.

location.anchor_text: Configurations are C1 R, C2 S, C3 S, C4 S, C5 R.

location.observation: The long_description states the anomeric carbon is R. The asset's own SMILES gives C1 = S under rdCIPLabeler (full set C1 S, C2 S, C3 S, C4 S, C5 R), which is the correct alpha assignment. R at C1 would be the beta anomer. The structure is right and the description of it is wrong. The sibling asset mol-alpha-d-glucopyranose states C1 S correctly, so this is an isolated transcription error.
location.learner_impact: Anyone reading the structured description rather than the picture - screen-reader users, anyone checking their own CIP assignment against it - is told the alpha anomer has the R configuration at C1 in the one section of the chapter that is entirely about telling alpha from beta. It is also a wrong-chemistry error that lives only in the accessibility channel, so a sighted proofreader comparing the drawing to the title will never see it.
location.evidence: mol-alpha-d-mannopyranose accessibility.long_description 'Configurations are C1 R, C2 S, C3 S, C4 S, C5 R'; RDKit rdCIPLabeler on the asset SMILES returns anomeric = S.
location.recommended_outcome: The structured description of this figure needs to report the configuration the drawn structure actually has, and the descriptions of the other stereochemical figures need the same machine check applied.

location.anchor_text: This is the same stabilization, in its extreme form, that the previous section identified as the anomeric effect

location.observation: concepts[].prerequisites for glycoside-formation lists only ['anomers-and-mutarotation'], but the nugget's expanded prose explicitly builds its central mechanistic argument on the anomeric effect, which is introduced in pyranose-chair-conformation (order 7). A learner following the declared prerequisite graph - or a course that skips the advanced-difficulty chair section - arrives at glycoside formation without the concept the explanation leans on.
location.learner_impact: The declared prerequisite graph drives concept maps, adaptive sequencing and instructor pick-and-choose. Because pyranose-chair-conformation is the chapter's only advanced concept, it is precisely the one an instructor is most likely to drop - and dropping it silently breaks the mechanism story in the next section.
location.evidence: concepts[] glycoside-formation prerequisites: ['anomers-and-mutarotation']; nugget-glycoside-formation expanded references the anomeric effect by name as a callback.
location.recommended_outcome: The dependency the prose actually creates between the anomeric effect and glycoside formation needs to be visible in the concept graph, or the glycoside mechanism needs to stand on its own.

location.anchor_text: Convert a Fischer projection to a Haworth projection using the right-to-down rule

location.observation: Three stated learning objectives are never assessed at the level at which they are stated. (a) Both haworth items set positions = [1], so the student only places the anomeric H/OH; no item asks for the C2/C3/C4 faces of a whole sugar. (b) Both chair items reduce to one shared label for all substituents at once, so the per-position alternation the nugget calls 'the single most common error in the conversion' is never tested. (c) The Fischer-to-wedge-dash conversion and the worked R/S assignment showing D-glyceraldehyde is (R) are taught at length and never assessed.
location.learner_impact: The three skills the chapter itself flags as the highest-risk are the three the bank cannot detect a student failing. A student can pass this bank while being unable to draw a Haworth projection of glucose or a chair of glucopyranose.
location.evidence: ch25-haworth-beta-anomer and -v2 positions = [1]; ch25-beta-glucose-chair and -v2 answer_key [redacted]; nugget-fischer-projections objective 3 has no corresponding item.
location.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs assessment that reaches the full conversion skills its objectives claim - placing every substituent in a Haworth drawing, and calling axial versus equatorial position by position on a chair.

location.anchor_text: Acetylation converts the free secondary hydroxyls at C2, C3, and C4 into esters and does not touch the anomeric carbon

location.observation: Both the flawed_work passage and the keyed correct repair enumerate the acylatable hydroxyls of methyl alpha-D-glucopyranoside as C2, C3 and C4, omitting the primary hydroxyl at C6. Acetic anhydride/pyridine acetylates the C6 primary alcohol fastest of all four. The keyed repair therefore states an incomplete and, as written, incorrect product. The chapter's own prose has it right.
location.learner_impact: The item is about reasoning carefully from the structure in front of you - the accessible_description even says 'hydroxyl groups on three other ring carbons', reinforcing the miscount. A student who correctly notices the C6-OH and expects a tetraacetate is told the right answer is a triacetate.
location.evidence: ch25-glycoside-error-repair-v2 flawed_work and repair_options fix_unchanged; contradicted by nugget-glycoside-formation expanded: 'The hydroxyls at C2, C3, C4, and C6 are ordinary primary and secondary alcohols'.
location.recommended_outcome: The item's inventory of acylatable positions must match the structure it displays and the chapter's own prose, including the C6 primary alcohol.

location.anchor_text: This one is worth reasoning through rather than dismissing.

location.observation: feedback_bundle.wrong_answer_explanations contains an entry matched to a specific option_id, and that option_id [redacted] is in answer_key.correct_option_ids. Every other wrong_answer_explanation in the chapter is keyed to a genuinely incorrect option. Either this explanation fires when a student selects a correct answer, or the match never resolves and the chapter's best piece of teaching feedback on the ketose/enediol route is dead content.
location.learner_impact: The fructose case is the single most instructive item in this section. If the explanation misfires it contradicts the grader; if it never fires, the student gets no correction.
location.evidence: ch25-reducing-sugar-select answer_key [redacted]; wrong_answer_explanations includes a match on option_id 'c'.
location.recommended_outcome: Feedback intended for a student who omits a correct multi-select option needs a delivery mechanism distinct from wrong-answer feedback.

location.anchor_text: D-Ribulose has five carbons, a ketone carbonyl at C2

location.observation: None of the ten authored practice_check items reaches the compiled reader, and none of the 31 asset long_description texts does either. Molecule blocks carry only alt_text and the short description (the asset learning_goal). Ten well-written self-checks and 31 structured descriptions exist in the package and are invisible to the student.
location.learner_impact: The chapter's only in-line retrieval practice is absent from the surface the reader actually uses, so the reading experience is ten blocks of continuous exposition with no checkpoints. The structured descriptions, which carry the CIP assignments, are likewise unreachable.
location.evidence: topic.package.json defines practice_check for all 10 nuggets and long_description for all 31 assets; the compiled reader contains neither.
location.recommended_outcome: The authored self-checks and the structured figure descriptions need a delivery path into the reader.

location.anchor_text: close the resulting seven-membered ring, label it as strained and unfavourable

location.observation: The video brief instructs the animation to label the seven-membered ring from C6 attack as 'strained'. The nugget expressly rejects that framing: the ring is 'neither strained enough to be impossible nor favourable enough to compete: the ends of a seven-membered chain meet rarely'. The corresponding question feedback also says 'forms slowly', not 'strained'.
location.learner_impact: If produced as briefed, the animation would contradict the prose and the question feedback, and would reinforce the wrong model that all medium rings are strained rings. The distinction between entropic and enthalpic disfavour is one of the more transferable ideas in the section.
location.evidence: video_briefs video-ring-closure storyboard step 4; nugget-cyclic-hemiacetal-formation expanded; ch25-ring-closure-arrow wrong_answer_explanations.
location.recommended_outcome: The video's stated reason for rejecting the seven-membered ring needs to match the reason the chapter gives.

location.anchor_text: less than 0.02 percent of dissolved glucose is open-chain at any moment

location.observation: The open-chain population of aqueous glucose is quoted at four different precisions across the chapter: 'less than 0.02 percent', 'Fewer than two molecules in ten thousand', 'well under one molecule in a thousand', 'well under 0.1 percent', and 'far below one percent'. All are true as upper bounds; the measured value is about 0.003 percent. The concept trouble_spot quotes yet another form.
location.learner_impact: A student comparing the reader against the figure caption or the trouble-spot list sees numbers spanning a factor of fifty for the same quantity and cannot tell which is the fact to remember.
location.evidence: nugget-cyclic-hemiacetal-formation terse and expanded; nugget-anomers-and-mutarotation standard and expanded; rc-mutarotation long_description; concepts trouble_spots.
location.recommended_outcome: One consistent figure for the open-chain fraction across prose tiers, figure descriptions and trouble spots.

location.anchor_text: gives x = 0.36 for the alpha fraction; measured directly, the equilibrium in water near 31 C is about 38 percent alpha and 62 percent beta

location.observation: The prose performs the weighted-average calculation, gets 36 percent alpha, then states the measured value as 38/62 and attributes the gap to trace furanose forms. The question keys 63.7 percent beta with a tolerance of 2. A student who has memorised the chapter's headline 62 is inside tolerance by 0.3, but one who rounds to 61 or 60 fails. The chapter's own 38/62 figure is never the keyed answer to the question built on it.
location.learner_impact: The most-repeated number in the section sits at the very edge of the tolerance band of the item that computes it.
location.recommended_outcome: The relationship between the two-component calculated composition and the directly measured one needs to be unambiguous where the item is graded.

location.anchor_text: Dihydroxyacetone: the only achiral ketose

location.observation: The asset title claims dihydroxyacetone is 'the only achiral ketose' and the long_description that it is 'the only monosaccharide' with no stereocenter. Both are unqualified absolutes that are only true inside the chapter's implicit restriction to 2-ketoses of three to six carbons. A 3-ketopentose with opposing configurations at C2 and C4 is meso and achiral, and glycolaldehyde is an achiral diose with no stereocenter.
location.learner_impact: The chapter is otherwise scrupulous about flagging where a rule has exceptions. An unqualified 'only' in a figure title is the kind of claim a student will reproduce on an exam and be marked down for.
location.evidence: assets[] mol-dihydroxyacetone title and long_description; compare nugget-carbohydrate-classification expanded, which states the fact without the absolute.
location.recommended_outcome: The uniqueness claim needs the scope it is actually true within - the common 2-ketoses - rather than being asserted over all ketoses and all monosaccharides.

location.anchor_text: a monocarboxylic acid that can no longer close a six-membered hemiacetal ring

location.observation: The figure's learning_goal says the aldonic acid 'can no longer close a six-membered hemiacetal ring', while the nugget two paragraphs later says 'Aldonic acids readily cyclize to five- or six-membered lactones.' Both statements are correct - a lactone is not a hemiacetal - but nothing in the chapter makes that distinction explicit, and the two sentences read as a direct contradiction.
location.learner_impact: Students already conflate hemiacetal, acetal, ester and lactone; presenting 'cannot close a ring' and 'readily cyclizes' within one section without naming the difference invites the wrong resolution.
location.recommended_outcome: The chapter needs to make explicit that the ring an aldonic acid forms is a lactone rather than a hemiacetal.

location.anchor_text: The hydrogen on atom 3 (carried implicitly in the drawing)

location.observation: The four atom_labels use ids 1-4 that do not correspond to the atom indices of the supplied molecule_smiles: for O=CCCCCO the aldehyde carbon is index 1 but the carbonyl oxygen is index 0 while being labelled '2', and the hydroxyl oxygen is index 6 while being labelled '3'. Label '4' names a hydrogen that the parenthetical concedes is not drawn. The chemistry of the four keyed ledger rows is entirely correct.
location.learner_impact: A student cross-referencing the label list against the displayed structure finds that the numbering is a separate scheme from the drawing, and that one of the four labelled atoms is not present in the drawing at all.
location.evidence: ch25-hemiacetal-bond-ledger molecule_smiles 'O=CCCCCO' with atom_labels ids 1-4 described in prose; expected_rows reference atom pairs '3-4' and '2-4'.
location.recommended_outcome: The atoms a student is asked to reason about must be identifiable in the structure they are shown, including the transferred proton.

strengths: Stereochemical fidelity of the monosaccharides is excellent: all 30 molecule SMILES machine-verified with rdCIPLabeler, and 29 of 30 carry exactly the configuration their title, alt text and prose claim - including alpha- versus beta-D-glucopyranose, beta-D-galactopyranose, alpha-D-mannopyranose, beta-D-ribofuranose, beta-D-fructofuranose with its quaternary anomeric carbon, both methyl glucosides, and 2-deoxy-D-ribose where the CIP descriptor legitimately flips relative to ribose.

All four disaccharides survive in-silico hydrolysis against verified references, with the correct anomeric configuration of the donor ring in all four and the dual-anomeric 1-to-2 linkage of sucrose right. This is the thing carbohydrate chapters usually get wrong.

The chapter states its alpha/beta rule against the sugar's reference arm rather than as 'beta is up', and explicitly claims the arm-based version survives translation to furanoses. Tested in 3D: in beta-D-fructofuranose the anomeric OH does sit on the same face as the C6 arm. The pedagogical claim is not just careful, it is correct.

Numeric claims check out across the board: rotations for glucose and galactose, sucrose inversion, the 0.9 kcal/mol A-value and the 20 percent it predicts, 2^n stereoisomer counting, amylose's 6-residue helix, amylopectin's 25-residue branching and glycogen's 3-fold denser branching.
Two easily-missed alditol subtleties are handled correctly: ribitol is labelled without a D- prefix (confirmed meso) while D-arabinitol is correctly treated as chiral.
Assessment breadth is genuinely strong: 28 base items plus 28 variants across 19 question types, every one of the 10 concepts assessed, and the type choices are apt.

Two defect classes that recurred in earlier chapters are fixed here: error_repair answer keys carry both the target_id and expected_target forms, and every numeric_with_units tolerance uses the {mode, amount} dict shape.

The Kiliani-Fischer synthesis_route items are chemically exact - D-arabinose verified, the gluco cyanohydrin correct, the partial reduction correctly specified, and the epimeric pairs correctly stated.

The prose repeatedly builds mechanism rather than asserting outcome: the entropic argument for intramolecular hemiacetal formation, the planar-carbonyl argument for mutarotation, the n-to-sigma* geometry of the anomeric effect, and the ring-flip cost argument for galactose's axial C4.
open_questions: Does any delivery surface shuffle option, card, or matching-row order at render time? No shuffle/randomise/Math.random found in the renderers, which is why instr-004 is rated high - if shuffling happens server-side before payload assembly, that finding drops to low.
How does the grader treat a wrong_answer_explanations entry whose match resolves to an option that is in correct_option_ids (ch25-reducing-sugar-select, option [redacted])?
Is the non-delivery of practice_check and long_description to the compiled reader a tracked platform gap, or specific to this compile?
Can the haworth question type accept a full set of ring positions, or is the single-position form a renderer limitation that constrains what instr-007 can ask for?

In ch25-anomeric-effect-reasoning the distractor e_mp ('The axial anomer has the higher melting point') is not merely irrelevant but factually false for glucose (alpha 146 C, beta 150 C), and the feedback rebuts it only on relevance grounds. Should a false distractor be corrected as false?

findings.summary: The prose in this chapter is, sentence for sentence, some of the friendliest I have read: it names the mistake I am about to make before I make it, it justifies rules instead of just stating them, and the hint ladders on nearly every question genuinely go from strategy to narrowing to specifics rather than restating the prompt. But what I actually receive as a reader is 8,000 words of continuous text illustrated by thirty generic skeletal structures, with no checkpoint, no objective list, no summary, and - in a chapter whose entire spine is three named drawing conventions - not one picture of a Fischer projection, a Haworth projection, or a chair. The Haworth-to-chair conversion, which the text itself calls 'the single most common error in the conversion,' is asserted rather than worked, illustrated by nothing, and assessed by a question that hands me the answer in its own prompt. Every one of the ten authored practice_check items is missing from the compiled reader, so I go from reading straight to graded questions with nothing in between. On top of that, a comparison-matrix cell requires me to answer that free glucose survives prolonged 1 M NaOH, which is the opposite of what two other sections of this same chapter teach me - so studying the chapter makes me get that item wrong. And because the three detail tiers are alternatives rather than a sequence, a student who picks 'terse' or 'standard' to reduce the load loses facts the questions grade on: the ketose-stereocenter rule, the Kiliani-Fischer sequence, the anomeric-effect bond-length evidence, and the weighted-average rotation calculation are all expanded-only.

location.anchor_text: Forgetting this - assuming up means axial - is the single most common error in the conversion

findings.observation: The Haworth-to-chair conversion is stated as a rule and then its result is asserted, never derived, and the chapter contains no drawing of a chair or of a Haworth projection to check the assertion against. The prose tells me the up direction 'alternates between axial and equatorial as you go around the ring' and that an up group at C1 and an up group at C2 'have different labels,' then immediately reports the finished answer without ever showing which ring carbons make up axial and which make up equatorial. The one asset assigned to this step, video-fischer-to-haworth-to-chair, compiles into the reader as a video block with an empty url. The only chair question, ch25-beta-glucose-chair, removes the step entirely by telling me the answer in its prompt and grades a single label, 'equatorial'.
findings.learner_impact: This is the point where I stop. I am told this is the mistake everyone makes, I am given the corrected rule in one abstract sentence, I am shown no picture of either drawing, and then the only exercise hands me the answer. I cannot check whether I can do the conversion, so I memorise 'beta-glucose is all-equatorial' as a fact and guess on anything else - which is exactly the failure the section says it is preventing. When a later question or an exam asks me for galactose or mannose, I have no procedure to fall back on.
findings.evidence: nugget-pyranose-chair-conformation expanded text, paragraphs 2-3; concept objective 1 'Translate a Haworth projection into a chair conformation'; trouble_spot 1 of the same concept; assets[] contains 30 molecule assets and 1 reaction_coordinate and no chair or Haworth figure; compiled reader block for video-fischer-to-haworth-to-chair has url empty; ch25-beta-glucose-chair prompt_text and answer_key expected_label equatorial.
findings.recommended_outcome: A student needs to see the Haworth-to-chair mapping carried out position by position on at least one sugar - which face becomes axial and which equatorial at each numbered ring carbon - and needs at least one exercise that requires performing that mapping rather than being told its outcome. Right now the chapter's own declared hardest step is neither demonstrated nor assessed.

location.anchor_text: Survives prolonged treatment with 1 M aqueous NaOH at room temperature

findings.observation: The comparison_matrix ch25-anomer-comparison-v2 requires the cell f_base / case_sugar to be marked 'Applies' - i.e. that free beta-D-glucopyranose survives prolonged treatment with 1 M aqueous NaOH at room temperature. Two other sections of this same chapter teach the opposite. nugget-glycoside-formation (expanded) says glycosides 'survive basic conditions that would epimerize or isomerize a free sugar', and nugget-sugar-oxidation-and-reduction (expanded) says 'free reducing sugars left standing in base scramble their configuration at C2'. The question's own level-3 hint reinforces the wrong reading: 'Neither compound has an acidic proton or a leaving group that hydroxide can act on' - but the free sugar's C2-H in the open form is precisely the acidic proton the enediol section is built on.
findings.learner_impact: A student who read the chapter carefully and remembered its most repeated warning about base gets this cell wrong; a student who read nothing and guessed 'both survive' gets it right. That is the single most demoralising thing an assessment can do to someone with low confidence - it teaches me that studying does not help and that I should answer by pattern rather than by reasoning. Worse, the graded key installs the misconception the chapter spent a paragraph dismantling.
findings.evidence: ch25-anomer-comparison-v2 answer_key [redacted]; feedback_bundle.hints[2] 'Neither compound has an acidic proton or a leaving group that hydroxide can act on.'; contrasted with nugget-glycoside-formation expanded and nugget-sugar-oxidation-and-reduction expanded ('the same enediol converts a sugar into its C2 epimer, so free reducing sugars left standing in base scramble their configuration at C2').
findings.recommended_outcome: The row's claim and its key must stop contradicting the chapter's own teaching about what base does to a free reducing sugar - either the property being compared has to be narrowed to something that genuinely is true of both, or the expected cell has to match what the prose teaches. As it stands the answer is unreachable from the chapter.

location.anchor_text: A ketohexose therefore has one fewer stereocenter than an aldohexose of the same length.

findings.observation: The rule that decides several questions - in a ketose the carbonyl carbon is not a stereocenter, so a ketose has one fewer stereocenter than the aldose of the same chain length - appears in exactly one place in the whole chapter: the expanded tier of nugget-carbohydrate-classification. The word 'stereocenter' does not occur anywhere in the terse or standard tier of that nugget, and nugget-d-l-configuration-and-families never mentions ketoses in connection with counting stereocenters at any tier. Yet ch25-rank-stereocenter-count is marked difficulty 'core' and cannot be ordered correctly without it, ch25-count-aldohexose-stereoisomers-v2 is built entirely on it, and the practice_check for nugget-carbohydrate-classification asks for the stereocenter count of D-ribulose.
findings.learner_impact: On a question labelled 'core' - the ones I attempt first because they are supposed to be the safe ones - I hit a discriminating rule I have never been shown unless I happened to be reading the longest tier. The hint ladder tells me 'Terminal CH2OH groups and carbonyl carbons never qualify', which is the rule, but by then I have already answered and been marked wrong.
findings.evidence: String 'stereocenter' present in nugget-carbohydrate-classification only in the expanded tier; nugget-d-l-configuration-and-families never pairs 'ketose' with stereocenter counting at any tier; ch25-rank-stereocenter-count difficulty 'core'.

Wrong-answer explanations on the single- and multi-select items teach the criterion rather than asserting the key - ch25-assign-d-or-l explains for each distractor which stereocenter was inverted and why that one does not decide the letter.
The prose names common wrong moves before I make them and explains why they are wrong, not just that they are.

Importance is signposted honestly, including the unusually candid 'It is a plausible account rather than a proven cause, and it should be offered as such' about glucose's biological prevalence.
Each new relationship is tied back to one I already have instead of being introduced as a new species - 'anomers are simply epimers at one particular carbon'.
The generic_incorrect_explanations on the multi-part questions, though not per-cell, are written as procedures I can rerun.
open_questions: Is the empty video url in the compiled reader a per-chapter authoring gap or a platform-wide delivery gap? Every one of the compiled reader chapters shows the same empty-string pattern, which suggests platform - I have reported ss-012 at medium rather than high on that basis.

findings.summary: The prose layer of this chapter is the strongest non-visual chemistry writing I have reviewed here: all three projections (Fischer, Haworth, chair) are taught as explicit verbal rules, and at every detail tier the text states which side of a Fischer projection each D-glucose hydroxyl sits on, which face each Haworth substituent occupies, and which chair positions are axial or equatorial. All 168 hints are text; every selected-response option, matching item, categorize item and rank card carries a real text label rather than a 'Structure A/B/C/D' placeholder; bond_change_ledger ships a fully described non-visual workspace; and the automated leak guard flags 0 of 56 questions. The figure and question layers do not match that standard. Every figure ships a rich atom-by-atom long_description, but the compiled reader carries only alt_text, and the alt_text for 17 of 31 assets is identical modulo the compound's name. Both hotspot questions expose atoms only as 'C atom 5' RDKit indices with no connectivity, both structure_scaffold questions are a bare Ketcher iframe the registry itself marks not keyboard-complete with no alternative and no disclosure, and both curved_arrow questions render only the molecule-click path, which emits a source kind the answer key cannot match while the labelled site-select fallback that IS the declared non-visual mode never renders. Fifty-four of the 56 authored accessible_description strings are never displayed to any learner.

strengths: The prose carries all three representations in words, at every detail tier. nugget-haworth-projections states the conversion rule and then applies it carbon by carbon, and nugget-pyranose-chair-conformation names the axial/equatorial outcome for four named sugars explicitly. A non-visual learner can determine every one of these from the text alone.

The terse and standard detail tiers both retain the load-bearing rules (horizontal-toward/vertical-away, right-becomes-down, up-stays-up-but-changes-name, beta-is-on-the-C6-arm-face). A learner using a reduced-density tier as a cognitive accommodation loses none of those rules.
All 168 hints across the 56 questions are kind text. There is not one image-only, highlight-only or animation-only hint in the chapter.

Every selected-response option, categorize item, matching item, rank card, comparison-matrix case and synthesis-route intermediate carries a real text label. The 'Structure A/B/C/D' anti-pattern that broke ch15 and ch16 does not appear anywhere.

Both bond_change_ledger items are a model of non-visual authoring: reaction_display narrates the transformation in prose, atom_labels names each of the four participating atoms in words, and the renderer exposes them as a labelled list plus a labelled editable table.

The Fischer and Haworth builders are genuinely keyboard-complete, and this chapter uses them in the mode where that holds - per-stereocenter and per-face selects alongside the drag affordance rather than instead of it.
find_accessibility_leaks flags 0 of 56 questions; I ran it directly against the authored package. Descriptions consistently state the stimulus and the task and stop there.
The four deferred videos are compiled with is_hidden true and an empty URL, so no learner meets a dead player, and each production_note records its accessibility requirements up front.

No meaning in the chapter rests on colour, motion or hover. The only colour language in the prose is genuine chemistry - the Benedict's blue-to-brick-red transition and the Tollens' silver mirror - and it is always paired with the underlying redox statement.
open_questions: Is this chapter intended to ship with no Fischer, Haworth or chair figure at all? Several long_descriptions are written as though such figures exist (access-010).

Does anything outside ReactionCoordinateQuestionRenderer plan to consume accessible_description? Findings access-003, access-004 and access-007 would all be materially reduced if the authored descriptions were rendered.

The chair grader accepts expected_label if the set of submitted orientations has exactly one member - which appears to score correct when only one of the five substituents has been placed. I could not confirm whether normalize_chair_state requires full placement.
I did not verify behaviour of the two hotspot items under a live screen reader - my conclusion in access-003 is from the rendered aria-labels and the enrichment payload, not from an AT session.
No new category identifiers were coined; every finding uses a value already listed in finding-schema.md.

findings.summary: This chapter is written with unusual care about spatial relationships and then declines to draw a single one of them. Ten sections carry 53 figure cards, 30 of them distinct, and every one is an RDKit skeletal depiction of a single compound; the one non-molecule figure is the mutarotation energy profile. Three of the ten concepts - fischer-projections, haworth-projections, pyranose-chair-conformation - are about representations that the chapter never renders. Five figure captions actively describe a drawing that is not on screen. The chapter's single energy diagram renders alpha and beta glucopyranose at identical energy with identical barriers, contradicting both its own alt text and the 38/62 equilibrium the prose derives. Layout compounds this: the compiler emits exactly one text block per section followed by a bank of 4-8 figures, so no figure is ever adjacent to the sentence it supports. Two multiple-choice items illustrate only the correct option, which is a visual answer tell independent of any chemistry. Against that, the asset alt texts are honest about what is actually drawn, the hotspot items are genuinely answerable from the depiction, and the alpha/beta comparison matrix isolates the difference correctly.

location.anchor_text: The anomeric configuration of the 1,4 linkage between glucose units

findings.observation: In ch25-cellulose-vs-starch exactly one of four options carries a structure_smiles, and it is the key (option a, cellobiose). The identical pattern appears in ch25-glycosylation-outcome-v2, where only option a is illustrated and option a is the key. Both survive compilation into compiled/question-set.json unchanged.
findings.learner_impact: A learner scanning the option panel sees one option with a picture and three without. The illustrated option is selectable on layout alone, with no carbohydrate reasoning at all. This rewards visual pattern-matching over the concept and produces a score that does not report understanding - and it is invisible to a text-only answer-leak check because the tell is graphical.
findings.evidence: ch25-cellulose-vs-starch: options a/b/c/d, structure_smiles present only on a; answer_key [redacted]. ch25-glycosylation-outcome-v2: structure_smiles present only on a; answer_key [redacted].
findings.recommended_outcome: The visual treatment of options must not correlate with correctness: either every option in a set is illustrated or none is. The need is that the picture panel carry no information about which option is right.

location.anchor_text: C2 epimers, and therefore diastereomers

findings.observation: In ch25-epimer-relationship and ch25-glycosylation-outcome, two of four options carry a structure_smiles and the other two do not; the key is one of the two illustrated options in both cases.
findings.learner_impact: The illustrated pair narrows a four-way choice to a two-way guess before any chemistry is read. A learner who works visually will notice the asymmetry immediately; one who works from the text will not, so the same item is easier for some students for reasons unrelated to the objective.
findings.evidence: ch25-epimer-relationship: illustrated ['a','b'], plain ['c','d'], key 'a'. ch25-glycosylation-outcome: illustrated ['a','b'], plain ['c','d'], key 'a'.
findings.recommended_outcome: Illustration must be uniform across an option set, or absent. The need is that no learner can shorten the search space by looking at which options have pictures.

location.anchor_text: at every stereocenter, the horizontal bonds point toward the viewer and the vertical bonds point away

findings.observation: The Fischer section spends 594 words defining a cross with a viewer convention, then walks three spatial manipulations, then does an R/S assignment that turns on which arm the lowest-priority H sits on. Its figures are RDKit line-angle depictions with no vertical spine, no horizontal arms, and no cross. Nothing anywhere in the chapter draws a Fischer projection.
findings.learner_impact: Every operation described is a change to a picture the learner has never seen. The learner is then asked to produce one in ch25-build-d-glucose-fischer, whose builder workspace is the first Fischer cross in the entire chapter and appears inside a graded item.
findings.evidence: nugget-fischer-projections asset_ids = ['mol-d-glyceraldehyde','mol-d-erythrose','mol-d-threose','mol-d-glucose-open']; all four compile to block_type 'molecule' with skeletal SMILES.
findings.recommended_outcome: The learner needs to see a worked Fischer projection - the spine, the four rows, and at least one of the three manipulations performed on it - before the first item that asks them to build one.

location.anchor_text: as a hexagon for a pyranose or a pentagon for a furanose

findings.observation: The Haworth section gives four explicit drawing conventions plus the right-means-down / left-means-up conversion rule applied carbon by carbon to D-glucose. Its five figures are RDKit ring depictions that satisfy none of the four conventions and encode face information as wedge/dash rather than up/down.

findings.evidence: nugget-haworth-projections prose lists the four conventions as bullets; asset_ids resolve to five molecule blocks.
findings.recommended_outcome: The learner needs at least one Haworth projection drawn to the conventions the section states, and the glucose-versus-galactose C4 contrast shown as the single flipped vertical line the prose describes.

location.anchor_text: No other common aldohexose can do this.

findings.observation: This is the longest section in the chapter (827 words) and it is entirely about geometry a flat depiction cannot express: up alternating between axial and equatorial around the ring, all five substituents equatorial, galactose forced to carry C4 axial, mannose carrying two axials, and the anomeric effect's antiperiplanar requirement. Its five figures are flat RDKit ring drawings. No chair is drawn anywhere in the chapter.

findings.evidence: nugget-pyranose-chair-conformation asset_ids = five molecule assets; package contains no chair-kind asset.
findings.recommended_outcome: The learner needs the all-equatorial beta-D-glucopyranose chair shown with its positions labeled, and at least one contrast shown against it, before the section's stability argument can be checked rather than believed.

location.anchor_text: places every substituent equatorial

findings.observation: Five asset learning_goal strings - which the compiler emits into the reader as the visible caption line under each figure - describe features of a representation that the rendered image is not. mol-d-erythrose: 'both carry the hydroxyl on the right in a Fischer projection' (no Fischer projection is rendered). mol-beta-d-galactopyranose: 'one hydroxyl on the opposite face of the ring'. mol-beta-d-xylopyranose: 'places every substituent equatorial'. mol-alpha-d-mannopyranose: 'two of its substituents are forced axial in either chair'. mol-alpha-d-glucopyranose: 'the anomeric hydroxyl sits on the opposite side of the ring from the C6 arm'.
findings.learner_impact: A learner who reads the caption and then looks at the picture to confirm it finds nothing that matches. The caption implies the axial/equatorial information is present in the drawing, so a learner may believe they are failing to read a figure that in fact does not contain the claim. The alt texts on the same assets are accurate about the skeletal drawing, so the caption and the alt text describe two different images.
findings.evidence: topic.package.json assets learning_goal fields; compiled reader molecule blocks carry content.description = learning_goal.
findings.recommended_outcome: Every caption must describe what is actually on screen. Either the figure must become the representation the caption names, or the caption must be rewritten to claim only what a skeletal depiction shows.

location.anchor_text: about 38 percent alpha and 62 percent beta

findings.observation: rc-mutarotation is the chapter's only relationship figure and it renders inline. But the spec supplies two steps with equal default magnitude (1.0) and identical barrier 'large'. The renderer computes minima as 0.0, +1.6, 0.0 and both peaks as max(flank)+2.0, so the drawn curve puts alpha-D-glucopyranose and beta-D-glucopyranose at exactly the same energy with two barriers of exactly the same height. The figure's own alt_text says beta lies just below the alpha anomer; the section's prose derives 38 percent alpha / 62 percent beta.
findings.learner_impact: The one diagram in the chapter that shows a relationship rather than a compound shows the wrong relationship. A learner reading the curve concludes the two anomers are isoenergetic and that neither step is rate-determining - directly contradicting the paragraph beside it and the alt text under it. Separately, ch25-mutarotation-profile asks the learner to identify a rate-determining step from a profile with unequal barriers, a profile shape the reader never showed them.
findings.evidence: rc-mutarotation.spec.steps = [{endergonic, large},{exergonic, large}] with no magnitude; [internal source reference — not in this repo]: DEFAULT_STEP_DROP 1.6, magnitude default 1.0, peak_e = max(left_e, right_e) + BARRIER_HEIGHTS['large'].
findings.recommended_outcome: The drawn profile must encode the two facts the section teaches: beta below alpha, and a first barrier the learner can see is the higher one. The need is that reading the curve give the same answer as reading the paragraph.

findings.evidence: ch25-haworth-beta-anomer student_config [redacted]; [internal source reference — not in this repo] draws stubs inside positions.map(...) only.

location.anchor_text: The reader carries the same content in nugget-haworth-projections and nugget-pyranose-chair-conformation.

findings.observation: All four video briefs are production_status 'deferred' and compile to video blocks with url empty and is_hidden true, so the reader shows no moving media. location.anchor_text: the way to keep them straight is by asking which end of the chain each one reaches

findings.observation: The compiler emits exactly one text block per section - 536 to 989 words - followed by the section's entire figure bank. findings.observation: The reader emits 53 molecule blocks for 30 distinct assets - 23 repeats, every one a byte-identical depiction with an identical caption. beta-D-glucopyranose appears 6 times, open-chain D-glucose and alpha-D-glucopyranose 4 times each. findings.evidence: Compiled reader: 53 molecule blocks, 30 distinct names; beta-D-Glucopyranose appears in six sections.

findings.evidence: nugget-d-l-configuration-and-families asset_ids lists 8 molecule assets; compiled section has 8 consecutive molecule blocks.

personas.executive_summary: Chemically this is the strongest chapter reviewed in this series so far - the instructor persona machine-verified all 30 asset SMILES and all 34 distinct question structures, hydrolysed all four disaccharides in silico, and found 29 of 30 structures and every numeric claim correct, including the dual-anomeric sucrose linkage that carbohydrate chapters normally get wrong. It is nevertheless BLOCKED, on nine persona blockers in four groups. (1) Two verified wrong-chemistry defects: mol-beta-d-xylopyranose ships the ALPHA anomer, disproving the caption, the prose and a question key that all depend on it being all-equatorial; and a comparison_matrix cell keys 'free glucose survives prolonged 1 M NaOH', which the same chapter refutes two sections later via the Lobry de Bruyn-van Ekenstein rearrangement, so a student who read the chapter is marked wrong. (2) Two items that cannot be answered correctly by anyone: both curved_arrow questions expect a lone_pair source while the renderer emits site.kinds[0] = 'atom', and both chair items score full marks for placing a single substituent. (3) A graphical answer tell - two single_select items illustrate only the key - which is the ch15 defect class recurring, invisible to the text-only leak guard. (4) Required-access blockers: hotspot atoms are exposed only as RDKit indices ('C atom 5' is sugar C1) with no connectivity, and structure_scaffold offers a Ketcher iframe the registry itself marks not keyboard-complete, with no alternative and no disclosure. Beneath the blockers sit two structural themes all four personas reached independently: the chapter teaches three drawing conventions (Fischer, Haworth, chair) and draws none of them, and an entire authored layer - 10 practice checks, 31 long descriptions, 54 of 56 accessible descriptions - never reaches any learner because no renderer consumes it.
consensus_strengths: Stereochemical fidelity: 29 of 30 asset SMILES and all four disaccharides verified correct in sugar identity, linkage carbon and anomeric configuration (Instructor, machine-checked).
Every numeric claim checks out - rotations, equilibrium compositions, the 0.9 kcal/mol A-value, polymer branching frequencies, 2^n counting (Instructor).
The chapter states the alpha/beta rule against the sugar's own reference arm rather than as 'beta is up', and that formulation was verified correct in 3D on a furanose (Instructor).
All 168 hints are text; no image-only, colour-only or motion-only hint anywhere; no meaning rests on colour or motion (Accessibility).
Every option, card, matching item and matrix case carries a real text label - the 'Structure A/B/C/D' anti-pattern from ch15/ch16 does not recur (Accessibility).
Hint ladders genuinely escalate from strategy to narrowing to specifics rather than restating the prompt (Struggling Student).
The prose names common wrong moves before the student makes them and explains why they are wrong (Struggling Student).
Asset alt texts honestly describe the skeletal drawing that is actually rendered; the overclaiming is in the captions, not the alt text (Visual Preference).
The 5-hydroxypentanal / cyclic-hemiacetal pair is a well-chosen before-and-after that isolates ring closure from sugar stereochemistry (Visual Preference).

disagreements.topic: Whether the reduced detail tiers are safe for a learner who uses them as a load accommodation

positions.Accessibility Persona: 'The terse and standard detail tiers - which are alternatives, not summaries - both retain the load-bearing rules (horizontal-toward/vertical-away, right-becomes-down, up-stays-up-but-changes-name, beta-is-on-the-C6-arm-face). A learner using a reduced-density tier as a cognitive accommodation loses none of the chemistry.'
positions.Struggling Student: 'Because the three detail tiers are alternatives rather than a sequence, a student who picks terse or standard to reduce the load loses facts the questions grade on: the ketose-stereocenter rule, the Kiliani-Fischer sequence, the anomeric-effect bond-length evidence, and the weighted-average rotation calculation are all expanded-only.'

disagreements.resolution: Both are right about different things, and the distinction matters for the fix. Accessibility is correct that the four conversion RULES survive into every tier - I verified this. Struggling Student is correct that specific GRADED FACTS do not. The remedy therefore is not to rewrite the tiers wholesale but to move the handful of graded facts down into the shorter tiers (rec-012), which preserves Accessibility's finding that the tiers are a usable accommodation.

disagreements.topic: Whether naming an option after the compound helps or harms

positions.Accessibility Persona: access-007 wants a text equivalent attached to options whose discriminating feature is visible only in the drawing; access-008 simultaneously notes that naming the compound hands the answer away in two items.
positions.Learner with Visual Preference: vis-001/vis-002 want illustration made uniform across an option set, which pushes toward MORE structures rather than more text.

disagreements.resolution: Adopt both, at different layers: make illustration uniform (rec-004) so the picture carries no positional information, and attach the discriminating STRUCTURAL FEATURE - not the classification - to each option's text. That satisfies Accessibility's equivalence requirement without reintroducing the giveaway it flagged in access-008.

disagreements.topic: Severity of the empty video blocks and the undelivered practice checks

positions.Struggling Student: Rated ss-012 and ss-006 at medium, explicitly because the same empty-url pattern appears in every compiled reader chapter and therefore looks platform-wide rather than chapter-specific.
positions.Organic Chemistry Instructor: Rated the same non-delivery (instr-010) at medium but framed it as content that 'exists in the package and is invisible to the student', i.e. a real loss regardless of cause.

disagreements.resolution: Kept at high in the synthesis (rec-017). The personas correctly identified the cause as platform-level, but the learner impact is the whole retrieval-practice surface of the chapter plus its entire structured-description layer, which is a high-severity loss even when the cause is not chapter-local. Recording it at the severity of its cause would hide it.
